**Saturday, June 23, 1956**

The year you were born into was 1956, and 1956 was not an ordinary year. It was the year the old order began showing its seams simultaneously on multiple fronts — and the child born in June arrived at the exact center of that unraveling.

Four months before your birth, Nikita Khrushchev stood before a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party congress and delivered what became known as the Secret Speech. For hours he detailed Stalin's crimes: the purges, the show trials, the cult of personality, the terror. The speech was supposed to remain confidential. It leaked. Communist parties across the world went into shock. The Soviet system had built itself on a foundation it was now admitting, from within, was rotten. The child born that June arrived into a world where the ideological certainty of the Cold War's communist pole had already begun to crack — not from outside pressure, but by its own leadership's confession.

On the exact day of your birth — June 23, 1956 — Gamal Abdel Nasser was confirmed as president of Egypt by national referendum. He was thirty-eight, a former army colonel who had toppled the monarchy, and he was about to make his most consequential move. Six weeks after your birth, on July 26, Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal — the waterway through which much of the world's oil flowed, still operated as a colonial concession by Britain and France. Britain, France, and Israel invaded. Eisenhower forced them to withdraw. The lesson was stark: the European empires could no longer project military force in the Middle East without American permission. The old imperial order had not merely weakened — it had lost the ability to act unilaterally. The child born on June 23 entered the world on the day that sequence began.

Four months after your birth, Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. Hungary had risen in popular uprising; for several days the revolutionaries held the capital. Then the tanks arrived. Thousands died. Hundreds of thousands fled west. Khrushchev's Secret Speech had suggested the system might reform itself. Hungary demonstrated what happened when people tested that proposition against its steel edge.

Now two exact-date moments from later in your life.

**June 23, 1972** — your sixteenth birthday — President Nixon signed Title IX of the Education Amendments: thirty-seven words prohibiting sex discrimination in any federally funded educational program. It took years to implement and decades to contest, but it was the legal hinge that opened women's athletics, professional schools, and scientific training on terms the country had never offered before. You were sixteen on the day the law changed.

**June 23, 2016** — your sixtieth birthday — the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union. The Brexit referendum passed 52 to 48. The postwar European project — built across the whole span of your lifetime on the ruins of the catastrophes that predated your birth — fractured that evening. You were sixty years old on the night the result came in.

The arc of seventy years contains more than can be easily compressed. You were born into a world where the Salk polio vaccine had been announced just fourteen months before — parents were, for the first time in a generation, beginning to exhale. You were born as rock and roll was arriving: "Heartbreak Hotel" had spent eight weeks at number one by June 1956, and Elvis would scandalize The Ed Sullivan Show in September. Sputnik came the following year. The Space Age had not yet started; you were born just before it did.

In seventy years: the complete arc of the Space Age; the Civil Rights movement; the Moon landing; Nixon's fall; the personal computer; the AIDS crisis; the fall of the Berlin Wall; the Soviet Union's collapse; the internet; 9/11; a global pandemic; and now an AI revolution that is changing the nature of knowledge work itself.

The world you were born into was organized around certainties that have since dissolved: the permanence of European empire (ended by Suez, six weeks after your birth); the ideological solidity of Soviet communism (cracked by Khrushchev's own words before you were born, shattered in 1991); the stability of the Cold War's fixed boundaries (gone in 1989); and the durability of the postwar European project (fractured on your sixtieth birthday). Each of these structures shaped the world of your childhood. Each has since given way.

You were born into a world reorganizing itself under new pressures. Seventy years on, the reorganization has not stopped — and shows no sign of doing so.
